Reviewer #1:

Overall, this is an excellent paper. The careful use and description of the simulations is to be commended. The authors make several interesting observations about rates and accuracy of exon defined and intron defined splicing events. Their results are certainly the most complete treatment of gene structure and splicing in Drosophila. There are, however, a few issues that should be addressed.

1) The analysis makes the explicit assumption that transcription rates are uniform across genes. This is probably close to true for Drosophila but I would think that this could be tested using the data from these experiments and earlier ones from, for example, the Lis lab. I would be most concerned about how non-homogeneous transcription rates might affect some of the conclusions made regarding effects at the ends of genes.

2) A related issue is the unstated but important assumption that 4s-U labeling is instantaneous and uniform. There must be a lag, and perhaps a significant lag, in labeling, particularly in the 5-minute time point, during which the uridine pool is reaching a new equilibrium. There is significant literature on this issue in cultured cells (although perhaps not in S2 cells) from which to make reasonable approximations. From what I can tell, this effect was not modeled in the simulation and it is not clear to what extent this might affect the rates of splicing observed. While most of the analyses in the paper are comparative rather than absolute, the authors do make claims about real-time rates. They should address this point and perhaps show that their measured rates are valid when this issue is included.

3) The discussion of developmental and stress response genes being enriched for exon definition does not seem complete. Exon definition genes are longer and so take longer to transcribe. Splicing appears to be faster for such genes but what is the actual rate limiting step in their synthesis? It could even be 3' end formation rather than elongation or splicing.

4) The authors note that the first introns are often more slowly spliced than subsequent introns. What about last introns and, in particular, exon defined last introns that may rely on different mechanisms?

Reviewer #2:

This paper was a delight to review! By labeling nascent RNA transcripts with 4-tiouridine, the authors were able to infer which transcripts retained introns and which had already spliced out the introns. They allowed for modeling of the full dynamics of the splicing process to estimate rates of splicing of every intron in the transcriptome. The goal was to learn how intron and exon lengths impact splicing dynamics. The find that exon-spanning introns are more efficiently spliced than intron-spanning splice sites, and suggest that genes that require rapid activation (such as stress response) have evolved the exon-spanning definition. Also genes that are very highly expressed tend to use the exon definition mode, consistent with the need for faster transcript processing.

The paper is well written and very well motivated. Intron-defined and exon-defined splice sites are clearly spelled out, and the unknowns regarding relative use of these splicing kinetic pathways drive the need for studies like this. The use of 4-thiouracil (4sU) incorporation provided a means to estimate the half-life for the splicing time of essentially every intron in the 5600 most highly expressed genes.

The authors do a good job showing how the method will work in silico, through simulations of the 4sU labeling processes and the inferred splicing half-lives of introns obtained from labeled transcripts with and without introns spliced out.

By doing 5, 10, and 20 min labeling with 4sU, followed by RNA sequencing and supplementing this with RNA-seq data of mature transcripts. The relative ratio of intron-exon junction reads to exon-exon junction reads was highest at the 5 min labeling period and decreased rapidly to low levels at longer times The method would appear at first to rely heavily on the assumption that all transcription proceeds at 1.5 kb/min, a figure that has good empirical support for the average, but which likely varies considerably. Simulations do an adequate job showing that the splicing half-lives are nevertheless well estimated over a reasonably broad range of transcription rates (although presumably if transcription rate were related to splicing progress in some aberrant way, the method could falter).

The data presented here clearly supports the notion that short introns that have relatively long flanking introns will tend to employ the intron definition splicing mode, whereas those with longer introns than the average of the flanking exons will tend to employ the exon definition splicing mode.

One technical detail could be made a bit more clear. The Materials and methods section succeeds very well in describing the way that splicing kinetics are learned from the relative abundances of spliced and unspliced introns in transcripts of different lengths. The contrast of several methods for quantitative analysis is good, and makes the logic clear. But the way that the data provide inference of the distinction between the exon-defined and intron-defined splicing could be more clearly spelled out. It appears to be based solely on RIME value, and while this is a sensible starting point, one would like to know if there is any other confirmation of these calls. In other words, one would like to know error rates for this inference.

An overall assessment of goodness-of-fit of the decay model to data would be good to see.

Given the unusually slow kinetics of splicing of the first intron (which often hold enhancer elements), it does appear to be sensible to drop the first intron in the analysis of the factors that determine splice mode.

Arguments that the splicing modes are a product of natural selection are speculative and are not based on either comparative (interspecific) analysis or on population genetic analysis. The former seems more likely to be feasible, but would entail a radical increase in the work (and so is not recommended here!). And the latter cannot be done without a battery of S2-like cells from different lines, which don't exist. Probably the relatively low frequency of polymorphism in splice sites would erode the power of any population genetic approach. So the suggestion is to make clear in the wording about the claims of selection that these are speculative inferences not based on specific evidence of past action of selection. To this reviewer, this lack does not erode the value of the paper, and the speculative remarks about natural selection do help the reader understand the nature of the question and the meaning of the results.

The splicing dichotomy poses an evolutionary puzzle that might warrant some discussion. Namely, the data appear to support the idea that the splicing modes driven by the relative lengths of introns and flanking exons. But natural selection in turn can also adjust these parameters. So, is there any adaptive argument to be made why Drosophila are balanced between the use of both modes?

It is somewhat of a limitation that the entire study was done in S2 cells. Is there any hope of getting 4sU into whole organisms to get at tissue-specific characteristics?

There are a few issues that are not addressed and might be of interest. Drosophila make great use of alternatively spliced exons and yet alternative splicing gets very short mention in the paper. Similarly nested genes would be expected to have odd splicing dynamics, and it might be a good sanity check to see this. I expected to see more discussion of the super short introns (<50 bp) found in Drosophila – are they all intron-defined and super-rapidly spliced? Is it necessary to invoke different splicing machinery for these?

Reviewer #3:

Pai and co-workers investigated genome-wide splicing rates in Drosophila S2 cells and how these rates relate to different modes of splicing (i.e. intron and exon definition). For this, the authors employed metabolic labeling coupled to RNA sequencing, combined with elegant mathematical modeling. The study reports several interesting results, including a local maximum for splicing rates for 60-70 nt long introns (the most common length in Drosophila) and the unexpected finding that exons surrounded by very long introns are spliced the fastest and most accurately.

Overall, I enjoyed the manuscript and I do not have any major concern. The following are specific comments/suggestions:

1) The fact that introns with similar rates tend to more often co-occur within the same genes seems to make sense. However, I wonder whether this could be driven, at least in part, by the different elongation rates among genes. If I understood it correctly, the model they developed assumes a single elongation rate for all genes. Therefore, it is possible that some gene-level biases are introduced because of this. While this should not affect most of the conclusions in the study, the bias may be strong enough as to create patterns of significant co-occurrence within genes (all introns within a gene will have the same bias and this will be different to most other introns). This is of course difficult to test. Perhaps the authors could use their data, consisting of three time points, to roughly estimate elongation rates and group genes based on these. Irrespectively, I may be a good idea to add a brief note about it.

2) Figure 4B: given the results in Figure 4C, it would be good to also have a comparison of half-life SDs for randomly sampled introns within groups of similar lengths, to see if this is the main feature driving the signal (rather than gene co-occurrence).

3) Subsection “Exon definition is associated with faster and more accurate splicing” and Figure 3C: this plot and the associated description in the text are not very easy to understand. The reference to stripes is ambiguous. I do not have a better suggestion on how to represent the data, but at least the wording in the text could be improved. It may help to label/highlight the sections of interest in the plot.

results.result: The junction dynamics approach outperforms other methods for estimating splicing rates from 4sU-seq data. In simulations, it achieved high correlation with true half-lives (rSpearman=0.95, rPearson=0.95), differed by only 21% on average from simulated values, and showed no detectable bias across the full range of half-lives. In contrast, the Ψ decrease method consistently overestimated half-lives, and the intron ratio method showed poor correlation (rSpearman=0.57).
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 provide comprehensive simulation-based validation of the junction dynamics method. The method shows strong performance in both relative ordering and absolute estimation of half-lives, with quantitative metrics demonstrating superiority over alternative approaches. The simulation framework appears rigorous and the results are internally consistent.

results.result: Application of the junction dynamics method to 4sU-seq data from Drosophila S2 cells yielded splicing half-lives for 25,576 constitutive introns in 5,608 genes. The median intron half-life was 2.0 min, consistent with co-transcriptional splicing given typical gene transcription times of 2-6 min. Estimated half-lives were robust to transcription rate assumptions, varying by only ~10% for rates between 1-3 kb/min.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C45 describe the experimental application and results. The median half-life of 2.0 min is reasonable given the transcription time estimates and is consistent with cited literature on splicing kinetics in other organisms. The robustness analysis (C45) strengthens confidence in the estimates despite the assumption of constant transcription rate.

results.result: Introns of 60-70 nt length are spliced most rapidly (median t½=1.7 min), representing a local maximum in splicing rates. Ultra-short introns (40-50 nt) are spliced more slowly (median t½=2.7 min) due to weaker 3' splice sites and suboptimal branch point sequence (BPS) positions. The peak at 60-70 nt may have been shaped by selection for efficient splicing, as natural selection favors short intron lengths in Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C46-C55 present a coherent story about the relationship between intron length and splicing rate at the short end of the distribution. The mechanistic explanation for slower splicing of ultra-short introns (weak splice sites, suboptimal BPS position) is supported by data (C50-C52) and is biologically plausible. The evolutionary interpretation (C54-C55) is reasonable given the data and cited evidence for selection on intron length.

results.result: Exon-defined introns (RIME>1) are spliced faster and more accurately than intron-defined introns (RIME<1). For exon-defined introns, longer intron lengths (>2944 nt) are associated with faster splicing, while for intron-defined introns, longer lengths (>99 nt) are associated with slower splicing. Exon-defined introns show enrichment of 6mers in flanking exons but not intronic regions, and have lower frequencies of non-canonical splice site usage, suggesting improved accuracy.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C59-C68, C72-C74 present a major finding about differential kinetics and accuracy of exon vs. intron definition. The opposite effects of intron length on splicing rate in the two modes (C63-C64) is striking and well-supported by data. The motif enrichment patterns (C66-C68) and accuracy measurements (C72-C74) provide mechanistic insight. The inference that exon and intron definition have fundamentally different kinetics (C65) is well-justified.

results.result: Splicing rates show unexpectedly low variation across introns within the same gene compared to randomly sampled introns. Multiple gene-level variables are associated with splicing rate, including gene expression level, first intron length, and splice site strengths. Intron length contributes positively to splicing rate for exon-defined introns but negatively for intron-defined introns. Genes with consistent splice site recognition modes show more uniform splicing rates than mixed-definition genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C75-C87 describe gene-level influences on splicing rates. The statistical evidence for lower within-gene variation (C83-C84) is strong (p<2.2×10⁻¹⁶). The regression analysis identifying multiple contributors (C75-C82) appears sound, though the R² values of 19.9% and 16% indicate substantial unexplained variance. The observation about consistent vs. mixed definition genes (C86-C87) is interesting and well-supported.

results.result: First introns are longer and spliced more slowly than other introns in Drosophila. Longer first introns are associated with faster splicing of downstream introns (rspearman=-0.06, p=0.00034), and genes with more introns have longer first introns. This suggests that gene architecture, particularly first intron length, impacts splicing efficiency of all introns in a gene, possibly by allowing time for recruitment of factors that promote downstream splicing.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C97 describe first intron effects. The data on first intron length and splicing rate (C88-C89) are clear. The correlation between first intron length and downstream intron splicing rates (C92) is weak but statistically significant. The mechanistic interpretation (C95-C96) is speculative but reasonable. The observation that genes with more introns have longer first introns (C97) supports the proposed model. Overall, the claims are well-supported though some interpretations are speculative.

results.result: Genes with exon-defined introns are enriched for developmental processes and stress responses, while intron-defined genes are enriched for RNA processing and metabolic processes. The enrichment for developmental and stress response categories increases with the proportion of exon-defined introns. This suggests that developmental and stress response genes may have evolved exon definition to take advantage of faster and more accurate splicing.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C111-C116 present functional enrichment analysis linking gene architecture to biological function. The Gene Ontology enrichment results (C111-C113) appear robust. The evolutionary interpretation (C7, C116) is speculative but reasonable given the observed faster/more accurate splicing of exon-defined introns and the biological importance of timing in development and stress response (C114-C115). The speculation is clearly labeled as such.

results.result: Alternatively retained introns and introns flanking alternatively skipped exons are spliced significantly more slowly than constitutive introns (Mann-Whitney p<0.01), independent of intron length. This suggests that the capacity for splicing regulation may impose limits on splicing rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 describe slower splicing of alternative introns. The statistical evidence is clear (p<0.01) and the observation is consistent with prior literature in mammalian systems (C32). The interpretation (C58) is reasonable though somewhat speculative. The result is well-supported.

results.result: Specific 6mers enriched in exons flanking exon-defined introns match known splicing factor binding motifs, including motifs for Pasilla/Nova (AACAAC, CAACAA, ACAACA) and SR proteins (GCAGCA). Longer exon-defined introns are preceded by upstream exons with higher density of significant 6mers.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 provide specific examples of enriched motifs and their correspondence to known splicing factors. The comparison to Pasilla/Nova binding sites (C69) and SR protein motifs (C70) is well-supported by citations. The observation about motif density (C71) provides additional mechanistic insight. These claims support the broader finding about motif enrichment in exon-defined introns.

results.result: Genes with mixed modes of splice site recognition have less consistent splicing rates than genes with predominantly intron or exon definition. There are 5% fewer genes with mixed modes than expected by chance (permutation test p<0.001), suggesting a tendency for introns in the same transcript to use the same recognition mode, possibly due to reduced availability of snRNPs after initial pairing.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C110 describe patterns in splice site recognition mode consistency. The observation about variance (C107) is supported by data. The statistical test showing fewer mixed-mode genes than expected (C110) is rigorous. The mechanistic explanation (C108-C109) is reasonable and supported by citation. The result is well-supported.

results.result: In 92% of genes expressed in Drosophila S2 cells, the half-life of the last intron is longer than the expected time to transcribe the last exon, making splicing likely to be rate-limiting for expression of a large portion of these genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 compare splicing and transcription times to infer rate-limiting steps. The calculation is straightforward and the conclusion (C118) follows logically from the data (C117). This provides important context for the biological significance of splicing kinetics.

results.result: Introns in genes with higher expression levels have faster splicing rates. By analogy to codon usage optimization in highly expressed genes, highly expressed genes may have evolved exon definition to boost splicing speed and spliceosome recycling efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 describe the relationship between gene expression and splicing rate. The observation (C119) is supported by regression analysis. The analogy to codon usage (C120-C121) is speculative but clearly labeled as such and provides an interesting evolutionary hypothesis. The speculation is reasonable given the data.

results.result: The predominance of short introns in Drosophila may result from mutational bias toward deletions, while the peak at 60-70 nt may reflect selection for efficient splicing. Selection for splicing speed/accuracy may maintain long introns in some genes despite mutational pressure. Possible mechanisms for faster exon definition include increased time for recognition/proofreading during transcription of long introns, tethering to polymerase, and SR protein involvement.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C106 present evolutionary and mechanistic interpretations. The mutational bias (C98-C99) is well-supported by citations. The interpretation about selection (C100, C103) is reasonable but speculative. The mechanistic explanations (C104-C106) are highly speculative, though based on reasonable biological principles and some cited literature. These claims represent interesting hypotheses but lack direct experimental support in this study.
